projects.title: Study Finder Chatbot
projects.description: We developed a chatbot tailored to assist international undergraduate students in finding suitable study courses in Germany. This chatbot serves as an intuitive interface for students to interact with, engaging them in personalized conversations to gather information about their interests, qualifications, and preferences. Leveraging advanced algorithms, the chatbot then matches students with relevant study programs, considering factors such as language of instruction, mode of study, financial considerations, and academic interests. By providing personalized recommendations and guidance, the chatbot aims to streamline the process of finding the ideal study program, ultimately enhancing the educational journey of international students in Germany.

activity.title: Picture this: You get a task from your manager or a homework assignment for class. To get it done quickly, you go to your smartest friend: an LLM. You ask one question. Five new concepts appear. You suddenly realize there’s a lot you don’t know… And even more, you didn’t know you didn’t know. So you keep asking follow-ups. Soon you hit an annoying reality: Either you cram everything into one tangled conversation, OR you scatter it across multiple chats and lose the big picture. You have two options. Either stack everything into one tangled conversation, or scatter it across multiple chats and forget how they relate to each other. Make your choice. (SAW voice) The end result? A graveyard of abandoned conversations you never scroll back to. That’s exactly why I built Arbor 🌳 - Arbor organizes LLM conversations as a **visual mind map** (or a tree as CS majors say) - Each chat becomes a node. - Follow-up questions become branches from their parent nodes. - You can label the connections between nodes to clarify how ideas relate (e.g. “implementation detail”, “counterexample”, “next step”). What makes it powerful: - When you're deep into a long chat and want to fork your thinking, Arbor gives you 3 precise ways to create a new branch: an AI-generated summary node (still experimental), a node built from the last 3 exchanges (for shorter or focused chats), or a node that copies the full conversation context. - For AI summarization, you can bring your own prompts and plug in your preferred LLMs, so the summaries match your workflow and level of detail. - Your API keys are stored locally in your browser, encrypted at rest, and never sent to any Arbor backend. - A full-page, interactive graph view lets you zoom out, explore, and navigate the entire conversation structure at once. - It currently supports the major LLM frontends many of us use daily: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity. I’ve also attached a short demo video showing how it works. If you use LLMs for studying, research, debugging, or complex decision-making, I’d love for you to try it and tell me what you think. Try Arbor here: https://lnkd.in/gkYNSjQY Feedback (good or brutal 😇) is very welcome. ...more

Who Said School Projects Have to Be Boring? Over the past four weeks, I took what was supposed to be a straightforward "To-Do List" assignment for my software course and transformed it into a fully functional Task Management Platform—with a twist. The theme? Attack on Titan. Because if I’m going to spend weeks staring at a task manager, it better be something I actually enjoy. But this project turned out to be so much more than just an assignment. It was a crash course in problem-solving, AI-assisted development, and making ambitious ideas actually work. 🔥 Lessons from the Battlefield (a.k.a. My Code Editor) 1️⃣ AI: Your Best Friend and Worst Anime Antagonist DeepSeek Reasoner R1, Claude 3.7, Cursor, Trae—these tools are incredible assistants. But here’s the hard truth: AI won’t think for you. It won’t choose the right tech stack, won’t debug logical issues for you, and won’t magically structure your project. Without truly understanding your architecture, logic, and feature requirements, you’ll end up spending hours (or days) writing code that breaks more than it fixes—when the solution was probably much simpler all along. 2️⃣ Think Like a User First, Developer Second The assignment was simple: make a basic to-do list with three levels of functionality. But instead of diving straight into writing code, I took a step back and asked: 💡 If I were actually using this every day, what would I want? This led me to go beyond checklists and CRUD operations and implement a feature set inspired by real-world productivity apps. Instead of just following the assignment specs, I made something I’d actually use. 3️⃣ Crazy Ideas? Go for Them. It took me exactly three reels to decide on an AOT-themed UI—but implementing it? That was like trying to navigate Shiganshina with no ODM gear. I had zero prior UI/UX experience, so every design choice felt like stepping into the unknown. But that’s the fun part—learning by doing. Now, I not only have a functional task manager but also a much deeper understanding of UI design and user experience. 🚀 What’s Next? This project didn’t just challenge me—it sparked something bigger. While working on it, I kept thinking about how task management could be taken to the next level. The ideas and lessons from this build have inspired a much larger project that I plan to develop as my graduation project next year. So, Notion , consider this a friendly warning—I’m coming for you. Or… maybe we should just join forces and redefine personal productivity together? (P.S. Still on the lookout for a summer opportunity! 👀) This project is far from perfect, but it taught me a ton—and I’d love to share more about it. If you’re curious about the project structure or want to check out the code, here’s the GitHub repo: 🔗 https://lnkd.in/dzuUwtFy ...more

One of the biggest takeaways from this project was mastering the balance between a user-friendly interface and powerful backend functionality. The dream of 8-year-old me is finally coming true. This fall, I will be joining the University of California, San Francisco for a PhD in Biological and Medical Informatics. When most kids in my third-grade dreamed of becoming pilots, engineers, or doctors, my answer was always a little different. I wanted to become a scientist. Science fascinated me, scientists were my role models, and I was never afraid of sounding different. Over the past four years, I have questioned that decision many times. Did 8-year-old Hassan really know what he was signing up for? Was that dream too naive? When so many people around me were pursuing high-paying careers in tech, I sometimes found myself doing two research internships in the same semester. I even went back to my roots and spent time working with labs in Pakistan, trying to understand how I could one day contribute to science there as well. Through all of those doubts came one very clear answer: I love research too much to leave it for anything else. I found my calling in asking questions that do not yet have answers, building things that may fail before they work, and contributing, even in a small way, to discoveries that could matter far beyond me. I am incredibly excited about this next chapter at UCSF and everything I still have to learn.

Earlier this May, I graduated from the University of Rochester with a Bachelor of Science in Electrical and Computer Engineering. I'm incredibly grateful to have been recognized with Highest Distinction from the University of Rochester Electrical and Computer Engineering , Magna Cum Laude honors, the Undergraduate Teaching Excellence Award, and The Faculty Award for Significant Contributions to the University Community. I also completed the University's TAKE5 Scholars Program, studying Psychology and Brain & Cognitive Science with a focus on growth mindset development in childhood, and graduated as an NAE Grand Challenges Scholar in the Engineering the Tools for Scientific Discovery track. Looking back on the past five years, I'm thankful for the opportunities that helped me grow, not only as an engineer, but also as a leader, mentor, researcher, and teammate. Some of the experiences I'm most proud of include: - Founding and leading the University of Rochester's first Remotely Operated Vehicle robotics team. - Co-leading the University's NASA Lunabotics team, where we designed and built an autonomous rover capable of operating in a simulated lunar environment and competed against graduate-level and top collegiate teams from around the world. - Spending two years conducting research in mobile manipulator autonomy and decentralized multi-robot collaboration. - Designing and building a Stewart platform-inspired robotic wrist for my senior design project, adding six degrees of freedom to existing robotic manipulators and developing a software interface compatible with industry-standard robotic arms (electronic PCB is on my gown cap!). - Serving as an undergraduate teaching assistant every semester since sophomore year, an experience that deepened both my technical understanding and my passion for helping others learn. - Inducted into Tau Beta Pi, the nation's oldest engineering honor society, in recognition of academic excellence and exemplary character. These experiences taught me that engineering is about much more than building technology, it's about collaborating with great people, embracing difficult challenges, and continuously learning. None of this would have been possible without the incredible professors, mentors, teammates, friends, and family who supported and challenged me throughout this journey. Thank you for believing in me and making these five years so meaningful. I'm excited to share that my next chapter has already begun. Last week, I joined NVIDIA as a Systems Software Engineer on the Behavior Planning team within the Autonomous Vehicles organization. I'm excited to learn from an amazing team and contribute to building the future of autonomous driving. Here's to new challenges, lifelong learning, and the journey ahead. #NVIDIALife #NVIDIA
